# Discussion

Returning to the hypotheses, the results provide partial support for
H1: the plant signal predicts valence above chance (macro-F1 = 0.42,
p = 0.005) and, although very weakly, the crossed emotion label
(macro-F1 = 0.21, p = 0.015), whereas arousal does not reach
conventional significance (macro-F1 = 0.36, p = 0.055). H1 is therefore
supported for valence and for the crossed emotion label, but not for
arousal.

The secondary analysis addresses a plausible alternative
explanation for that result. H2 is rejected, tested on valence as the
dimension for which H1 shows the strongest evidence. Both
branches of the confounding pathway are in fact present. CO~2~
correlates with valence ($\rho$ = 0.308, p \< 0.0001) and, in the raw
analysis, with most plant features, so the alternative explanation was
not implausible a priori. The decisive condition nonetheless fails: the
plant–valence association remains essentially unchanged once CO~2~ is
controlled for, so it is not an artifact of a shared dependence on
ambient CO~2~.

## Interpretation of our Findings

Valence is the target on which the positive claim of this study rests.
The winning model recognizes all three valence classes at comparable
rates, with per-class F1 scores of 0.43, 0.45, and 0.40
(@fig-cm-valence), so its macro-F1 of 0.42 does not arise from following
the largest class but from a discrimination spread across the entire
label space, and none of the 200 label permutations matched the observed
score (@fig-perm-valence). The effect is nonetheless small in absolute
terms: 43% accuracy against the approximately 33% expected by chance
with three classes. What the plant signal supports is therefore a
statistical association that becomes visible across 284 windows and 15
participants, not a channel from which the emotional state of an
individual person could be read off at a practically useful rate.

The feature ranking of that model indicates which properties of the
signal carry the association. The two highest-ranked predictors are
Hjorth mobility and complexity, dimensionless descriptors of how quickly
the voltage changes and how variable that rate of change itself is, and
Random Forest and XGBoost place the same pair at the top independently
of one another (@fig-imp-valence). The amplitude descriptors ranked
behind them, `plant_min` and `plant_range`, enter only in their
session-normalized form and therefore express how far a window departs
from the baseline of its own session rather than where that session lies
on the absolute voltage scale. The comparison of the two feature
representations is consistent with this. Session normalization raised
the average macro-F1 across the three classifiers by 0.031 for valence,
with the Random Forest gaining 0.068, and the best combination for this
target used session-normalized features. Since every recording session
contains exactly one participant, the absolute voltage level contained 
in the raw session data partly
encodes the session itself, carrying the ambient conditions of the
recording and the state of the electrode contact. That performance
improves once this level is removed indicates that the association is
carried by the dynamics of the signal rather than by properties that
distinguish one recording from another.

The crossed emotion label behaves differently. Its macro-F1 of 0.21 lies
close to the 0.20 expected from uniform guessing across five classes,
and the winning model attains its 42% accuracy almost entirely on the
dominant neutral class, with an F1 of 0.64 there against 0.07 and 0.08
for the two smallest classes (@fig-cm-emotion). Two effects work against
this target at once. First, crossing the axes distributes 284 windows
over five cells, leaving as few as 21 windows in the smallest of them,
so the minority classes are rare. Second, one of the two
constituent axes carries no usable signal: a label formed by crossing
valence with arousal cannot be more informative than its weaker
component, and arousal does not separate above chance. The crossed label
therefore does not aggregate the two dimensions; it combines an axis
that separates above chance with one that does not. The near-chance
emotion result is thus consistent with the valence result rather than in
tension with it, and supports treating valence and arousal as
analytically distinct targets rather than collapsing them into a single
categorical label.

Emotion is also the only target whose best combination uses raw
features, which does not reverse the general trend. The other two
classifiers improve under session normalization on this target as well,
XGBoost from 0.17 to 0.19 and the Neural Network from 0.18 to 0.19, so
the reversal is confined to the Random Forest, whose raw advantage rests
on the neutral class alone (F1 0.64 raw against 0.57 session-normalized)
rather than on any better separation of the minority classes. Given that
all six combinations fall between macro-F1 0.17 and 0.21, this
difference is within the variation among near-equivalent models.

Arousal is the weakest target, missing conventional significance at
p = 0.055 with 10 of 200 permutations matching or exceeding the observed
score (@fig-perm-arousal). This null result is difficult to attribute to
the plant, because valence and arousal were operationalized through
proxies of unequal quality: a facial expression model reading the
emotional display itself on the one side, a single index derived from
RMSSD and mean heart rate on the other. HRV markers of this kind track
emotional state reliably mainly for unpleasant and highly arousing
stimuli [@choi2017], while the video combines strongly negative segments
with mild, happy and neutral ones, so part of the recorded material falls
outside the range in which the arousal label is expected to be
informative at all. A weak label bounds the performance attainable by
any predictor of it, including a fully informative one. The arousal
result is therefore best read as uninformative about the plant rather
than as evidence against it.

The correlation analysis reports much weaker numbers than the
classification, and the two can easily be read as contradicting each
other. Within sessions, the average absolute correlation between a
single plant feature and valence is 0.07, and only 5 of the 22 features
reach significance, yet a classifier trained on those same features
reaches a macro-F1 of 0.42. The two quantities measure different things.
A Spearman coefficient asks whether one feature on its own rises and
falls with valence, whereas the classifier may use all 22 features at
once and split each of them at several thresholds, so it can exploit
combinations that no individual coefficient registers. The weak
correlations therefore do not undercut the classification result. They
indicate that the information lies in the combination of the features
rather than in any one of them.

Beyond rejecting H2, the CO~2~ analysis provides a further result.
Separating between-session from within-session variance distinguishes
the three edges of the confounding triangle. The plant--CO~2~ coupling
nearly disappears within sessions (mean $|\rho|$ = 0.067, significant in
3 of 22 features), identifying it as slow, room-level drift across the
recording day. The CO~2~--valence edge, in contrast, persists
undiminished within sessions ($\rho$ = 0.33, p \< 0.0001), which could be attributed to respiration changing alongside emotional state on a
timescale of minutes. Ambient CO~2~ therefore does track the
participant, but the plant does not track ambient CO~2~ on the timescale
at which the classification operates. Ambient CO~2~ is thus not a
plausible carrier of the valence information that is picked up by the classifier, and the mechanism behind the association remains open.

## Comparison with Previous Studies

The present study directly addresses the two central limitations that
@gloor2025 explicitly identified: the lack of a standardized elicitation
protocol and the single-subject design. By employing a fixed, ten-minute
video stimulus instead of post-hoc labeling of unconstrained behaviour,
and by recording 15 participants with grouped cross-validation to
prevent participant-level leakage, the present study constitutes a
multi-participant replication of this experimental paradigm with a
controlled emotion-elicitation protocol.

The shift from a binary "happy"/"sad" classification to a dimensional
valence-arousal framework [@russell1980] further extends this
replication methodologically: it allows for a more fine-grained analysis
than Gloor's binary scheme permitted, and reveals that plant signals are
informative for valence but not for arousal, a distinction that could
not have been captured within a binary classification framework in the
first place.

Both studies validate their findings via permutation testing, so neither
rests on cross-validation scores alone. A direct comparison of the
reported accuracies is nevertheless of limited value. @gloor2025 reports
72.8–73.8% at the optimal 1 s lag on a binary valence task (positive:
happy/surprise, n = 968; negative: fear/anger/sad/disgust, n = 651), a
60/40 split. That accuracy sits about 13 points above the majority
baseline he reports (59.9%), but his published confusion matrices show
the classifier leans heavily on the majority class: sad-class recall is
only about 0.52–0.57, giving a macro-F1 of about 0.71, slightly below
the headline figure. More important than the accuracy gap, the two
evaluation protocols differ in kind: our estimates come from
participant-grouped nested cross-validation, whereas Gloor uses
stratified k-fold on non-overlapping snippets without grouping by
session or day, so temporally adjacent snippets from the same 30-minute
session can fall in both train and test. His label-permutation test does
not rule this out, since shuffling labels leaves no session structure
for the null model to exploit. The three-class valence result here
(36–43%; chance about 33%) therefore cannot be placed on the same scale
as his within-subject binary figure, and the comparison supports little
beyond the coarse observation that both studies report performance above
chance.
